source.title: Everything You Always Wanted to Know About How Causal Set Theory Can Help with Open Questions in Cosmology, but Were Afraid to Ask

accepted.question_text: How did the universe begin, and how can a fundamentally discrete causal set description replace or explain the classical big bang singularity, a regime in which the continuum concept of spacetime ceases to be meaningful?

evidence.quote: How did our universe as we know it begin? The big bang is the conventional answer to this question provided by general relativity. Of course the big bang singularity represents a regime where the concept of spacetime ceases to be meaningful.

Causal sets, by virtue of their fundamental discreteness, evade such singularities. The minimum separation between the elements (presumed to be close to the Planck length) tames infinite curvatures and energies.

accepted.question_text: What first-principles mechanism, preferably arising from quantum gravity or causal set dynamics, can produce the early exponential expansion invoked to explain the universe's large size, high isotropy, homogeneity, spatial flatness, and lack of monopoles, without relying on an overly flexible inflationary model whose motivation is not fundamental?

evidence.quote: The first moments after the big bang are believed to consist of a period of exponential expansion. This is the best explanation we have for observations such as the large size of the universe, high degree of isotropy, homogeneity, spatial flatness, and the lack of monopoles.
However, the origin of this explanation requires explanation itself, and this is a current open question.
Inflation may in the future find its missing motivations if a theory of quantum gravity predicts a particular kind of it.

accepted.question_text: Classical sequential growth models are stochastic causal set dynamics in which a causal set grows element by element, with each new element choosing a random subset of existing elements as causal ancestors under rules preserving causality and a discrete analogue of covariance. Can any such dynamics eventually evolve into a manifoldlike causal set approximating a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker cosmological universe, and if so by what mechanism?

evidence.quote: A family of these models are known as ‘classical sequential growth’ or CSG models. As the name suggests, in these models, a causal set grows element by element sequentially.

Each new nth element selects a random subset of the existing elements to be in its causal past. While this choice is made randomly or stochastically, there are some rules to ensure that causality and a suitable analog of discrete covariance are preserved by the ancestor selection process.
A major open question is whether and how one of these dynamics eventually evolves into a manifoldlike causal set such as one approximated by a Friedman-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) universe.

accepted.question_text: What fundamental quantum-gravity-compatible model explains the detailed nature of primordial quantum fluctuations and how those fluctuations lead to structure formation, rather than relying on inflaton-field models that have not yet been naturally connected to a more fundamental theory?

evidence.quote: One of the successes of quantum field theory in curved spacetime has been to generate a primordial power spectrum that closely agrees with the observed anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background.
The detailed nature of these fluctuations and how they lead to structure formation is still not well understood.
As mentioned above, we would like to have a model that naturally connects to a more fundamental theory, and so far that has been challenging to achieve with inflation.

accepted.question_text: What observable cosmological consequences follow from using the Sorkin-Johnston state, a unique distinguished vacuum state that is well-defined for both causal sets and continuum curved spacetimes, to model quantum fields on cosmological backgrounds, especially when causal set de Sitter studies find new vacua and FLRW studies find super-horizon correlations without an inflation-like rapid expansion phase?

evidence.quote: Choosing a state in arbitrary curved spacetimes is a notorious challenge as there is no unique or obvious choice, and different choices lead to different consequences.

The Sorkin-Johnston (SJ) state is a choice of vacuum state in any arbitrary curved spacetime that is a candidate for circumventing this challenge. The SJ state is unique and distinguished in any globally hyperbolic spacetime and typically reflects the symmetries of the background spacetime (if there are any).

In the work in FLRW, correlations on super-horizon scales were found, without the help of a phase of rapid (inflation-like) expansion. It would be interesting to explore the phenomenological consequences of these findings regarding the SJ state.

accepted.question_text: Can covariant ultraviolet-cutoff predictions for primordial power spectra in quantum field theory on curved spacetime be realized or sharpened inside causal set theory, where Green functions, d'Alembertian operators, and an intrinsic covariant ultraviolet cutoff are available?

evidence.quote: There is also a recent direction of work that has made predictions for a signature of a covariant UV cutoff at the level of quantum field theory in curved spacetime.

Many of the ingredients of this work (e.g. Green functions and d’Alembertians) are available in causal set theory as well, in addition to it being a concrete example of a theory with an intrinsic and covariant UV cutoff.
It would be interesting to explore whether these predictions can be realized or sharpened in the context of causal sets.

accepted.question_text: What is the origin of dark matter, and can off-shell particles arising from causal-set-inspired nonlocal scalar quantum field theory provide a viable dark matter candidate, including a production mechanism in early-universe dense and hot conditions and potentially observable signatures despite zero non-gravitational scattering involving off-shell particles?

evidence.quote: The origin of dark matter, the mysterious dominant mass density in our universe, is a major open question in cosmology.
They found a set of on-shell and off-shell solutions in the mode expansion of the quantized field operator. These off-shell particles do not satisfy the conventional dispersion relation.
In other words, any scattering with off-shell particles has zero cross-section. This prompted them to consider these off-shell particles as a natural candidate for dark matter.
Specifically, post-inflation reheating and radiation self-interaction provide the dense and hot conditions that lead to efficient relevant scattering processes.
Despite this detection challenge, in Refs. 32 and 33 some potentially observable signatures of this model are suggested.

accepted.question_text: Can the causal-set nonlocal d'Alembertian field theories used for off-shell dark matter be extended beyond scalar fields to other kinds of fields, so that the framework is not limited to scalar-field propagation and scalar-field phenomenology?

evidence.quote: Nonlocal analogues of the d’Alembertian operator □ that describe the propagation of scalar fields, exist more commonly in causal set theory than their more conventional local counterparts.
Our discussion will be limited to scalar field theories. The extension to other kinds of fields is not presently known.

accepted.question_text: In the Everpresent Lambda model, causal set number-volume fluctuations and a volume-Lambda uncertainty relation yield Lambda approximately proportional to 1 divided by the square root of a spacetime volume V. Which spacetime volume V should be inserted into that relation, such as an observer's past-lightcone volume, and can that choice be justified from causal structure rather than imposed phenomenologically?

evidence.quote: Putting together (6) and (7) we have Λ = ΔΛ ∼ 1/ΔV. Finally substituting the variation of V from (5) we get Λ ∼ 1/√V.

The procedure above still leaves open the question of what volume to insert in (8). A causal choice would be to take the volume of our past lightcone, and this is indeed what is considered in the literature on Everpresent Λ.

accepted.question_text: Can causal set theory provide a fundamental reason for the Everpresent Lambda assumption that the mean value of cosmological-constant fluctuations is zero, instead of leaving zero mean Lambda as an input not derived from the fundamental causal set framework?

evidence.quote: Assumption 3: The mean value of Λ about which the fluctuations occur is zero.
This third assumption is the only input to the Everpresent Λ proposal that does not stem from a fundamental aspect of causal set theory.

accepted.question_text: Can current Everpresent Lambda models, or slightly modified versions of them, quantitatively alleviate both the Hubble tension in measurements of H0 and the S8 tension in measurements of matter clustering, without the common failure mode in which resolving one correlated tension worsens the other?

evidence.quote: The Hubble tension is the name given to a clash in recent measurements of the Hubble parameter H0, with disagreements between supernova (together with Cepheid stars and tip of the red giant branch) data and observations from the cosmic microwave background.
S8 ≡ σ8√Ωm/0.3 is the parameter used to quantify this tension, where Ωm is the fraction of the total energy density belonging to matter.
At present, there are only qualitative indications that Everpresent Λ possesses some of the features that are believed to be key to resolving the Hubble and S8 tensions.

Carrying out a dedicated and quantitative study of how much the current Everpresent Λ models (or slightly modified versions of them) can alleviate these tensions is one of the most important directions of future work on Everpresent Λ.

The S8 and Hubble tensions are correlated tensions, namely, many proposed models that alleviate one tension tend to worsen the other. Therefore it would be very interesting to see if Everpresent Λ can alleviate both at the same time.

accepted.question_text: What microscopic degrees of freedom or statistical-mechanical mechanism account for the entropy proportional to the area of cosmological event horizons, and can causal set theory identify this microscopic origin for cosmological horizon entropy?

evidence.quote: Not long after, these thermodynamic properties were extended to cosmological horizons (in models with a positive cosmological constant) as well.
Similar to the black hole case, these cosmological event horizons were also found to have a temperature and an entropy proportional to their area associated with them.
In this section we will focus on the outstanding question of: what is the microscopic origin of these (cosmological) horizon entropies?

accepted.question_text: Is the entanglement entropy of all quantum fields in nature, computed with causal set discreteness as a covariant ultraviolet cutoff and spacetime-correlator methods such as the Sorkin-Johnston vacuum, the complete microscopic explanation of horizon entropy or only one important contribution?

evidence.quote: In causal set theory, the entanglement entropy is expressed as a sum over solutions to a generalized eigenvalue problem involving the two-point correlation function of the theory, W(x, x′). The discreteness scale furnishes the covariant UV cutoff that makes this entropy finite.
Together with the SJ vacuum state, the application of this (entanglement) entropy definition in causal set theory in particular allows for the use of a fundamentally covariant UV cutoff.
Whether or not the entanglement entropy of all fields in nature turns out to be the full story of horizon entropy remains to be seen. It is, however, at the very least an important part of the story.

accepted.question_text: How do small-eigenvalue subtleties affect causal set calculations of de Sitter horizon entanglement entropy, and can the expected area laws be robustly revisited and extended to other spacetime dimensions and field theories?

evidence.quote: Specifically, causal sets approximated by 1 + 1 and 3 + 1 dimensional de Sitter spacetime were considered.
There are some subtleties involving small eigenvalues of iΔ that need to be handled with care, after which the expected area laws are obtained.
It would be interesting to revisit this problem in light of recent insights into the aforementioned subtleties. Extensions to other dimensions and field theories can also be explored.

accepted.question_text: Can horizon molecules, defined as linked causal set elements crossing a horizon, be formulated so that counting them yields finite and universal horizon entropy in higher-dimensional spacetimes and for null as well as spacelike hypersurfaces?

evidence.quote: These horizon molecules consist of linked elements with at least one element inside the horizon and at least one outside it.
It turns out that even in the causal set case one does not always obtain a finite number of any kind of horizon molecule, but there will be a finite number of particular kinds of horizon molecules.
Difficulties arising from extending the above simple case to higher dimensions led to the consideration of other kinds of horizon molecules.
However, they needed to require that Σ is strictly spacelike rather than spacelike or null. Ref. 69 showed that there are subtleties in the null case that spoil some of the encouraging results.

accepted.question_text: What cosmological observations could distinguish causal-set or other quantum-gravity effects from alternative explanations, given that a quantum theory may suggest or predict an effect without being unique in doing so and that contrived classical explanations may mimic the same observations?

evidence.quote: Cosmology offers a rich testing ground for approaches to quantum gravity.
There is no smoking gun evidence yet for any particular quantum gravity effect in cosmological observations.

Part of the challenge is that while a quantum theory may suggest an explanation for or even predict an effect, it is not unique in doing so; sometimes, one cannot even rule out a contrived classical explanation for the very same effects.
